concept.name: Bear raid
concept.definition: A market term for concerted heavy short selling of a stock, typically combined with spreading negative rumors about the company, intended to drive the price down quickly so the short sellers profit when covering at lower prices. When the selling is collusive or the rumors false, a bear raid constitutes market manipulation; heavy short selling based on genuine analysis is lawful.
concept.intuition: A pack of short sellers attacks a vulnerable company all at once — selling hard and whispering bad news — hoping to start a stampede they can ride to profit.
concept.mechanics: Participants quietly build large short positions in a target already under stress, then sell aggressively while circulating damaging claims (accounting fraud, imminent default, regulatory probes). Panic selling by other holders accelerates the decline; the raiders cover into the washout. The practice dates to the pre-1934 pool era and motivated early short-sale regulation such as the uptick rule.
concept.failure_modes: Falling prices are routinely blamed on bear raids when the real cause is bad fundamentals — distinguishing an attack from justified selling is often impossible in real time; collusion is usually only provable long after the fact through communications evidence.
concept.misconceptions: Not every coordinated-looking selloff or high short interest is a bear raid — short sellers frequently identify real problems, and lawful, independently motivated short selling plus truthful criticism is not manipulation; the illegal version requires collusion and/or false information.
concept.example: During the 2008 crisis, regulators examined whether concentrated short selling of Lehman Brothers and other financial stocks, coupled with false rumors of imminent collapse, amounted to bear raids — contributing to the SEC's temporary ban on short selling financial stocks that September.
